# anoa

> A real browser that takes commands. anoa is Chromium in one binary, driven from a shell, an HTTP endpoint, or any CDP client. There is no driver to install alongside it and no headless-versus-real distinction to reason about — `--headless` is a flag on the same executable.

The browser is the session. Every command attaches to a browser that is already
running and leaves it running, so the page, the cookies and the scroll position
survive between commands. That is what makes it usable one command at a time, by
a process that starts and exits, rather than only from inside a long-lived script.

`snapshot` returns refs (`@e1`, `@e2`) that later commands target, and clicks are
hit-tested — a button underneath a consent banner is reported rather than clicked
through. Both exist because the caller cannot see the screen.

Platforms: macOS (universal), Linux (x86_64 and aarch64, glibc 2.35+), Windows.
Also packaged as a Nix flake for x86_64-linux, aarch64-linux and aarch64-darwin
(`nix run github:porcupine-md/anoa-browser -- --headless --port 9222`); nixpkgs
has no qtwebengine for x86_64-darwin, so Intel Macs use Homebrew. Flakes are
still experimental, so a fresh Nix needs `experimental-features = nix-command
flakes` in ~/.config/nix/nix.conf before any of those commands work.
`anoa terminal` is POSIX-only. Latest release: v0.12.0.

## Start here

- [Install and CLI reference](/docs.html): every install path, every flag the browser takes, every command you can send it
- [Home](/): what it is, with screenshots of the live view and the terminal viewer
- [README](https://github.com/porcupine-md/anoa-browser#readme): the same ground plus the HTTP endpoints and CDP details
- [Releases](https://github.com/porcupine-md/anoa-browser/releases): prebuilt packages for every platform
- [Building from source](https://github.com/porcupine-md/anoa-browser/blob/master/docs/BUILDING.md): prerequisites, targets, release process

## The core loop

```bash
anoa --headless --port 9222 &     # start a browser, leave it running
anoa open example.com             # navigate (scheme optional)
anoa snapshot -i                  # interactive elements, with refs
anoa click @e2                    # act by ref, or by any CSS selector
anoa fill @e3 "user@example.com"
anoa get text                     # the page's visible text
anoa wait --selector ".results"
anoa screenshot page.png
```

Add `--json` to any command for machine-readable output. Exit codes: `0` ok,
`1` command failed, `2` usage, `3` no browser listening.

`anoa skills get commands` prints the full command reference to stdout, and
`anoa skills get core` prints the workflow — both meant to be read by an agent
rather than by a person.

## Commands

- Navigate: `open`, `back`, `forward`, `reload`, `wait` (`--load`, `--selector`, `--ms`, `--text`, `--url`, `--fn`, `--state hidden`, `--timeout`)
- Inspect: `snapshot [-i]`, `find role|text|selector [--nth]`, `get text|html|value|attr`, `eval`, `status`
- Interact: `click`, `fill`, `type`, `upload`, `press`, `scroll`, `mouse move|down|up|wheel`
- Capture: `screenshot [file]`, `pdf [file]`
- Tabs: `tab new [url] [--name] [--profile] [--isolated]`, `tab list`, `tab select`, `tab close`
- State: `cookies`, `storage local|session`, `set viewport|device|geo|offline|headers|media`
- Debug: `console`, `errors`, `network` — recorded inside the page, so they cover what happened before the command ran
- Agents: `skills list`, `skills get core|commands`, `close`

## Options

- Starting a browser: `--port`, `--headless`, `--no-sandbox`, `--width`, `--height`, `--profile`, `--profile-dir`, `--ephemeral`, `--download-dir`, `--extension`, `--auth-token`, `--embed-origin`, `--max-renderers`, `--proxy`, `--proxy-bypass`, `--config`

`--proxy` takes `host:port` or `scheme://host:port` (http, https, socks5,
socks4), with credentials in the URL; `--proxy-bypass` lists hosts that skip
it. The proxy belongs to the browser and every tab uses it — there is no
per-tab proxy, because Chromium keeps proxy settings per process and Qt
exposes none per page. Two proxies means two browsers on two ports.

Memory scales with tabs because Chromium runs a renderer process per tab:
measured, nine tabs cost 1031 MB of renderers against 117 MB for one, while the
browser process itself moved only 156 to 255 MB. `--max-renderers <n>` caps
that — 4 processes for 9 tabs was 468 MB — but tabs sharing a process share one
main thread, so nine tabs computing at once went from 469 ms to 1061 ms. It is
free when tabs are idle or driven one at a time, expensive when they all work at
once.
- Reaching one from a command: `--port`, `--host`, `--token`, `--tab`
- Terminal viewer: `--term-host`, `--term-port`, `--term-token`, `--cdp`, `--fps`, `--gfx`

`--tab` takes an id (`t2`) or a name given at creation (`--name search`), and
every command accepts it, so parallel work stays in its own tab.

## Ports

One number gives three. `9222` serves discovery (`/json`, `/json/version`,
`/json/list`) and the `/render/*` endpoints, and is what a client is pointed at.
`9223` is Chromium's own debugging port, kept internal, and serves the DevTools
frontend. `9224` is the CDP proxy — the WebSocket a client is handed lands there,
and it multiplexes sessions and checks the bearer token.

## Driving it over HTTP

No CDP client required. `/render` is a live view you can open in a browser or put
in an `<iframe>`: it streams a tab over MJPEG and forwards mouse and keyboard
back. `?tab=<id>` picks which tab a frame drives, `?embed=1` drops the built-in
chrome.

The rest of the family: `/render/screenshot.png`, `/render/screenshot.ppm`,
`/render/stream.mjpeg`, `/render/html`, `/render/viewport`, and for input
`/render/click`, `/render/move`, `/render/mousedown`, `/render/mouseup`,
`/render/scroll`, `/render/type`, `/render/key`, plus `/render/navigate`,
`/render/back|forward|reload` and `/render/tab/new|close`.

Two things to know before mapping coordinates: a captured frame is in *device*
pixels while every input endpoint speaks *logical* pixels, so on a HiDPI display
they differ by the device pixel ratio — ask `/render/viewport` rather than
measuring the image. And `dy` on `/render/scroll` is in angle-delta units where
negative scrolls down, roughly 60 px of page per 120-unit notch.

## Security

`--auth-token` is off by default and the `/render/*` endpoints carry no origin
check of their own, so on a shared or untrusted machine, set a token.

Framing the live view is opt-in by origin. It forwards keystrokes as well as
showing pixels, which means a page that can frame it can watch a logged-in
session and act inside it; the default is `Content-Security-Policy:
frame-ancestors 'self'`, and `--embed-origin` widens it.

## Compatibility

Playwright and Puppeteer connect unmodified:

```js
const browser = await chromium.connectOverCDP('http://localhost:9222');
const browser = await puppeteer.connect({ browserURL: 'http://localhost:9222' });
```

Also supported: `Page.printToPDF`, named profiles with isolated cookie jars and
localStorage, and unpacked Chromium extensions (manifest v2).
